steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on MV-ROPE, a multi-view RGB framework for category-level object pose and size estimation. It should motivate why depth-dependent methods are limited, explain the insights behind our approach, describe the system, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Problem: object detection and 6D pose and size estimation; instance-level vs category-level
- NOCS-based progress and the dependence on depth
- Motivation: three insights
- MV-ROPE framework overview
- Contributions
- Closing claim about experimental results

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Problem
  - detect objects, estimate 6D pose and size; robotics, augmented reality
  - instance-level: few exact shape priors (meshes, CAD models) -> model selection, correspondences, pose
  - category-level (this work): exact shape/appearance unknown; center, orientation, size at category level -> absolute pose and size
- NOCS and depth
  - Normalized Object Coordinate Spaces (NOCS) -> surge in research, better accuracy, wider real-world use
  - canonical representations from RGB, but robust estimation still needs depth for alignment
  - depth: direct depth channel or image-based prediction
  - depth cameras: partiality, artifacts; single-view prediction: misses details, absolute scale
  - RGB-D methods need high-quality depth; image-only methods not yet on par with state of the art
- Three insights
  - (1) accurate depth hard on consumer devices (iPhone, Azure Kinect), esp. small objects with smooth surfaces, intricate structures
  - (2) sensor often mobile, keeps gathering new views -> predictions from nearby images, incrementally improved over time
  - (3) motion stereo for dense depth -> no depth camera or single-view prediction needed
- MV-ROPE
  - scale-aware dense monocular SLAM + lightweight object pose estimator + object-level pose graph optimization
  - SLAM: monocular RGB sequence + scale info in; camera poses + dense metric depth out, dense bundle adjustment layer
  - estimator: pixel-wise canonical representations from RGB
  - registration of depth and canonical points -> object pose per keyframe
  - pose graph optimization over all keyframe poses -> accurate, robust 6D pose and size
- Contributions
  - first multi-view RGB framework for robust, accurate category-level pose; three modules, pose graph averages multi-view estimates; parallel, interactive level real-time
  - scale-aware monocular dense SLAM against scale invariance; inertial readings, stereo images, or RGB-D depth
  - images only: on par or better than RGB-D state of the art on public datasets; new dataset MEREAL, real-world RGB-D sequences, ground truth, different depth sensor types/qualities; benchmark for ours and prior RGB-D methods
- Closing: extensive experiments; superior when no direct depth or low-quality depth

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Detecting objects and estimating their 6D pose and size is an important problem for applications like robotics and augmented reality. In general the problem can be split into instance-level and category-level pose estimation. In instance-level estimation we assume we know a small number of exact shape priors (e.g. meshes, CAD models), and so the problem becomes discrete model selection, correspondence estimation, and pose estimation. This work looks at the more general case, category-level pose estimation, where the exact shape and appearance of the observed objects are assumed unknown. It defines the center, orientation, and size of objects at the category level, and in the end gives absolute pose and size estimations.

Since Normalized Object Coordinate Spaces (NOCS) were introduced {c}, there has been a surge of research in recent years, and the accuracy of category-level pose and size estimation keeps improving. These methods make object pose and size estimation much more applicable in real-world scenarios. However, NOCS methods can extract canonical object representations from RGB images, but robust object pose and size estimation still needs additional depth information to be integrated for accurate alignment. The depth information usually comes either as a direct depth channel reading or as image-based depth predictions. But it is well known that depth camera readings can easily suffer from measurement partiality or artifacts {c}, and single-view depth prediction may not reflect depth details or absolute scale accurately {c}. So current RGB-D based methods are limited in real-world applicability because they rely on high-quality depth sensing, and methods that only use images are not yet able to perform on par with the state-of-the-art.

Our work is motivated by three important insights: (1) Getting an accurate depth map is a practical challenge for consumer-grade devices such as the iPhone or Azure Kinect, especially for small objects with smooth surfaces and intricate structures. (2) In many practical applications we do not only have a single image taken of the environment; the sensor is often mobile and keeps gathering novel views of the scene. So we can continuously generate predictions from nearby images and improve the object pose predictions incrementally and robustly over time. (3) We can use motion stereo to do dense depth reconstruction, and so we do not need a depth camera or inaccurate single-view depth predictions.

- MV-ROPE
  - scale-aware dense monocular SLAM + lightweight object pose estimator + object-level pose graph optimization
  - SLAM: monocular RGB sequence + scale info in; camera poses + dense metric depth out, dense bundle adjustment layer
  - estimator: pixel-wise canonical representations from RGB
  - registration of depth and canonical points -> object pose per keyframe
  - pose graph optimization over all keyframe poses -> accurate, robust 6D pose and size
- Contributions
  - first multi-view RGB framework for robust, accurate category-level pose; three modules, pose graph averages multi-view estimates; parallel, interactive level real-time
  - scale-aware monocular dense SLAM against scale invariance; inertial readings, stereo images, or RGB-D depth
  - images only: on par or better than RGB-D state of the art on public datasets; new dataset MEREAL, real-world RGB-D sequences, ground truth, different depth sensor types/qualities; benchmark for ours and prior RGB-D methods
- Closing: extensive experiments; superior when no direct depth or low-quality depth

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Detecting objects and estimating their 6D pose and size is an important problem for applications like robotics and augmented reality. In general the problem can be split into instance-level and category-level pose estimation. In instance-level estimation we assume we know a small number of exact shape priors (e.g. meshes, CAD models), and so the problem becomes discrete model selection, correspondence estimation, and pose estimation. This work looks at the more general case, category-level pose estimation, where the exact shape and appearance of the observed objects are assumed unknown. It defines the center, orientation, and size of objects at the category level, and in the end gives absolute pose and size estimations.

Since Normalized Object Coordinate Spaces (NOCS) were introduced, there has been a surge of research in recent years, and the accuracy of category-level pose and size estimation keeps improving. These methods make object pose and size estimation much more applicable in real-world scenarios. However, NOCS methods can extract canonical object representations from RGB images, but robust object pose and size estimation still needs additional depth information to be integrated for accurate alignment. The depth information usually comes either as a direct depth channel reading or as image-based depth predictions. But it is well known that depth camera readings can easily suffer from measurement partiality or artifacts, and single-view depth prediction may not reflect depth details or absolute scale accurately. So current RGB-D based methods are limited in real-world applicability because they rely on high-quality depth sensing, and methods that only use images are not yet able to perform on par with the state-of-the-art.

Our work is motivated by three important insights: (1) Getting an accurate depth map is a practical challenge for consumer-grade devices such as the iPhone or Azure Kinect, especially for small objects with smooth surfaces and intricate structures. (2) In many practical applications we do not only have a single image taken of the environment; the sensor is often mobile and keeps gathering novel views of the scene. So we can continuously generate predictions from nearby images and improve the object pose predictions incrementally and robustly over time. (3) We can use motion stereo to do dense depth reconstruction, and so we do not need a depth camera or inaccurate single-view depth predictions.

We use these insights in a novel framework which we call MV-ROPE. It combines a scale-aware dense monocular SLAM module, a lightweight object pose estimator, and an object-level pose graph optimization module. The SLAM module takes a monocular RGB image sequence and additional scale information as input. It outputs accurate camera poses and also dense metric depth estimations through a dense bundle adjustment layer. The lightweight object pose estimator predicts pixel-wise object canonical representations from RGB images. We do geometric registration between depth and canonical object points and get the object pose in each keyframe. Then all keyframe object poses are optimized by an object-level pose graph optimization module. This lets us get accurate and robust 6D object pose and size estimations in the end. In summary, our contributions are the following:

- We present the first multi-view RGB framework for robust and accurate category-level object pose estimation. Its main modules are a scale-aware dense monocular SLAM module, a lightweight object pose estimator, and an object-level pose graph optimization module, which is used for averaging multi-view object pose estimations. These modules run in parallel and give robust estimations of canonical object pose and size in interactive level real-time.

- To get around the inherent scale invariance property of monocular SLAM, we propose a novel scale-aware monocular dense SLAM module that uses either inertial readings, stereo images, or direct depth readings from an RGB-D camera.

- Even when we only use images, our results show performance on par with or even better than previous state-of-the-art RGB-D methods on publicly available datasets. We also introduce a new dataset MEREAL that captures real-world scenarios, with RGB-D sequences and ground truth annotations from different types and qualities of depth sensors. This dataset is a benchmark for evaluating our proposed method and previously proposed RGB-D based algorithms.

Extensive experimental results show that our algorithm achieves superior performance when direct depth input is not available or when the depth readings are low-quality.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The detection of objects and the estimation of their 6D pose and size is an important problem in applications such as robotics and augmented reality. Generally, the problem can be divided into instance-level and category-level pose estimation. In the former, we assume knowledge about a small number of exact shape priors (e.g. meshes, CAD models), which reduces the problem to discrete model selection, correspondence estimation, and pose estimation. The present work looks at the more general case of category-level pose estimation, where the exact shape and appearance of the observed objects are assumed to be unknown. It defines the center, orientation, and size of objects at the category level, ultimately providing absolute pose and size estimations.

With the introduction of Normalized Object Coordinate Spaces (NOCS) [1], there has been a surge in research efforts in recent years, continuously improving the accuracy of category-level pose and size estimation. These methods significantly broaden the applicability of object pose and size estimation in real-world scenarios. However, while NOCS methods enable the extraction of canonical object representations from RGB images, robust object pose and size estimation still requires integration with additional depth information for accurate alignment. This depth information is commonly given either as a direct depth channel reading or as image-based depth predictions. Yet it is well-understood that depth camera readings may easily suffer from measurement partiality or artifacts [2], and that single-view depth prediction may fail to accurately reflect depth details or absolute scale [3]. Current RGB-D based methods are therefore intrinsically limited in their real-world applicability due to their reliance on high-quality depth sensing, while methods that purely rely on images are not yet able to perform on par with the state-of-the-art.

Our work is motivated by three important insights: (1) Obtaining an accurate depth map poses practical challenges for consumer-grade devices such as the iPhone or Azure Kinect, especially for small objects with smooth surfaces and intricate structures. (2) In many practical applications, we do not only have a single image taken of the environment; the sensor is often mobile and continuously gathers novel views of the scene. We may therefore continuously generate predictions from nearby images and incrementally and robustly improve object pose predictions over time. (3) We may rely on motion stereo to perform dense depth reconstruction and thereby bypass the need for a depth camera or inaccurate single-view depth predictions.

We exploit these insights in a novel framework, denoted MV-ROPE. It combines a scale-aware dense monocular SLAM module, a lightweight object pose estimator, and an object-level pose graph optimization module. Our SLAM module takes a monocular RGB image sequence along with additional scale information as input, and outputs accurate camera poses as well as dense metric depth estimations through a dense bundle adjustment layer. The lightweight object pose estimator predicts pixel-wise object canonical representations from RGB images. By performing geometric registration between depth and canonical object points, we obtain the object pose within each keyframe. All keyframe object poses are then optimized by an object-level pose graph optimization module, which allows us to ultimately obtain accurate and robust 6D object pose and size estimations. In summary, we make the following contributions:

- We present the first multi-view RGB framework for robust and accurate category-level object pose estimation. Our primary modules comprise a scale-aware dense monocular SLAM module, a lightweight object pose estimator, and an object-level pose graph optimization module, which is used for averaging multi-view object pose estimations. Running these modules in parallel yields robust estimations of canonical object pose and size in interactive level real-time.

- To circumvent the inherent scale invariance property of monocular SLAM, we propose a novel scale-aware monocular dense SLAM module making use of either inertial readings, stereo images, or direct depth readings obtained from an RGB-D camera.

- Even when relying solely on images, our results demonstrate performance on par with or even better than previous state-of-the-art RGB-D methods on publicly available datasets. Additionally, we introduce a new dataset MEREAL that captures real-world scenarios, including RGB-D sequences and ground truth annotations obtained from different types and qualities of depth sensors. This dataset serves as a benchmark for evaluating the performance of our proposed method and previously proposed RGB-D based algorithms.

We demonstrate through extensive experimental results that our algorithm achieves superior performance when direct depth input is unavailable or when using low-quality depth readings.

References:
[1] H. Wang, S. Sridhar, J. Huang, J. Valentin, S. Song, and L. J. Guibas, “Normalized object coordinate space for category-level 6d object pose and size estimation,” in Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition , 2019, pp. 2642–2651.
[2] M. Camplani and L. Salgado, “Efficient spatio-temporal hole filling strategy for kinect depth maps,” Proc SPIE , vol. 8290, pp. 13–, 02 2012.
[3] W. Yin, Y. Liu, and C. Shen, “Virtual normal: Enforcing geometric constraints for accurate and robust depth prediction,” IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence , vol. 44, no. 10, pp. 7282–7295, 2022.
